rationale: A wins because it gives the founder sharper reporting gates, especially the question of "which of the 50 countries actually support card issuance versus only reimbursement?" That is the kind of ugly detail that decides whether this becomes a real fintech story or a launch note. B is cleaner on grounding, but "Corporate Cards Were a US Startup Story. Now the Software Is Going Everywhere." is category wallpaper and partly repeats its incumbent-challenger angle. A has bruises, but it would keep a founder from walking into the pitch blind.
gaps_in_A: "multinational-payroll problem hits mid-size companies" drags in payroll and mid-size companies; the update gives corporate cards, expense management, reimbursement, enterprise demand, and startups, not payroll or a mid-market segment.

"Brex bets 50 countries is the thing Ramp can't copy quickly" is a punchy competitive frame, but the speed/copyability claim is not in the facts. It needs public Ramp footprint evidence before it leaves the building.

"distributed hiring made every Series B a multi-country employer" invents a remote-work/startup-operations trend the update does not prove. Funny how the refused list catches remote-work hallucination while this angle sneaks it back in through the side door.

"employees front costs on personal cards and wait on FX-mangled reimbursements" may be true, but it is not supplied. Keep it as a customer-interview question until a named finance lead says it on record.
gaps_in_B: "Corporate Cards Were a US Startup Story. Now the Software Is Going Everywhere." is too broad and overlaps with the first angle's challenger-versus-incumbent frame. Different altitude, yes; different story, barely.

"traditional issuers have long owned" and "historically been the incumbent advantage" are plausible, but still unsourced market-history claims. The update only says Brex competes with traditional corporate-card issuers.
"whether Brex's valuation can be sustained by revenue growth" imports a revenue-growth test without revenue facts. Good question, but do not let it masquerade as a sourced thesis.

"FX friction, and employee complaints about out-of-pocket costs" is useful color, not supplied evidence. B correctly asks for a customer, but the angle copy already talks like the customer has spoken.
